newsitem.title: USA: Former BATUS exec pleads guilty to wiretapping.
newsitem.headline: Former BATUS exec pleads guilty to wiretapping.

text.p: The former general counsel of BATUS Inc., once the holding company for Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp., pleaded guilty Thursday for his role in an illegal wiretapping conspiracy.

David Schechter, now chairman of Summit Capital Group Inc. in Louisville, Ky., faces a possible maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine. He is scheduled to be sentenced Sept. 15 in Manhattan federal court.
Louisville-based Brown & Williamson is now owned by B.A.T Industries Plc. BATUS was dissolved in the 1990s and its operations turned over to Brown & Williamson.
Schechter's 1995 arrest was part of the government's ongoing probe of the illegal sale of bugging and wiretapping devices and was not related to any investigation of tobacco companies.

As a result of the probe, federal authorities in March shut down the Spy Factory, the nation's largest chain of "spy shops," after the company and its owner pleaded guilty to smuggling and selling illegal bugging and wiretapping devices.

In the current case, prosecutors alleged that Schechter bought a sophisticated wiretapping device from a New York "spy shop" in December 1993 for $5,500 and agreed to pay $400 plus travel expenses to have the device installed in the Brown & Williamson Tower in Louisville.
The complaint alleges that on Jan. 23, 1994, an unidentified co-conspirator, who worked at the spy shop, flew from New York to Louisville and met with Schechter.
Prosecutors allege that Schechter brought the co-conspirator to another person's office at the Brown & Williamson Tower and showed him the telephone in which to install the wiretapping device.

The co-conspirator installed the transmitter into the telephone and also placed a receiver, designed to surreptitiously receive and record telephone calls made over the wiretapped phone, in Schechter's office.

The complaint also charged that the co-conspirator returned to Louisville three times between January 1994 and January 1995 to fix the device. Each time Schechter, who let him into the victim's office, paid the co-conspirator $1,200.
Schechter did not disclose during the plea hearing why he initiated the scheme and prosecutors also would not comment.
